prompt:
User: For bill-to/ship-to, is the place of supply where the goods are delivered?
Assistant: No, it is the principal place of business of the bill-to party who directs the delivery.
User: So if the bill-to party is unregistered, which address do I use?
completion: Use the address of the bill-to party's principal place of business as recorded with you, even if that party is unregistered. In a bill-to/ship-to sale the place of supply is the principal place of business of the person on whose direction the goods are delivered, and registration is not a condition. If that address is in another state from yours, charge integrated GST (IGST); if it is in your state, charge central GST (CGST) and state GST (SGST). Record the full address and state name on the invoice, as required for unregistered recipients when the value is Rs 50,000 or more. Reference: Section 10(1)(b) of the IGST Act, 2017 and Rule 46(e) of the CGST Rules.

prompt: A marketing agency has GSTINs in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, and Mumbai, Maharashtra. Its Mumbai team handles a client registered in Mumbai, but accounts wants to raise the invoice from the Ahmedabad GSTIN. What is the tax impact?
completion: Invoice from the Mumbai GSTIN and charge central GST (CGST) and state GST (SGST). The location of the supplier is the registered place from which the service is actually supplied, which is the Mumbai office. That makes the supply intra-state in Maharashtra. Billing from Ahmedabad would wrongly turn it into an inter-state supply with integrated GST (IGST) and put the tax in the wrong state. Each GSTIN is a distinct person, so if Ahmedabad staff help, Ahmedabad bills Mumbai separately. Reference: Section 2(15) of the IGST Act, 2017 and Section 25(4) of the CGST Act.

prompt: A software developer in Kochi, Kerala, builds an app for a client in Germany and receives Rs 18,50,000 in euros. Does she charge GST?
completion:
No GST is charged if she exports under a letter of undertaking (LUT). Her service is an export of services: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment in convertible foreign exchange, and the two parties are not merely establishments of one person. Exports are zero-rated.
Option 1: file an LUT and invoice Rs 18,50,000 with no tax.
Option 2: pay integrated GST (IGST) of 18,50,000 x 18% = Rs 3,33,000 and claim a refund.
Without an LUT she must use option 2. Reference: Section 2(6) and Section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017 and Rule 96A of the CGST Rules.

prompt: What is the place of supply for goods imported into India by a registered trader in Jaipur?
completion: The place of supply for imported goods is the importer's location, Rajasthan, and the tax is integrated GST (IGST) collected by customs. Imports are always inter-state, so central GST (CGST) and state GST (SGST) never apply at import. For example, assessable value plus basic customs duty of Rs 3,60,000 at 18% gives IGST of 3,60,000 x 18% = Rs 64,800 on the bill of entry. The trader claims that Rs 64,800 as input tax credit (ITC) once the bill of entry appears in GSTR-2B. Reference: Section 11(a) and Section 7(2) of the IGST Act, 2017, and Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

prompt: A chemical trader in Ankleshwar, Gujarat, booked an invoice dated 1 February 2026 for Rs 3,40,000 plus GST Rs 61,200 and claimed full ITC. By 31 July 2026 he had paid only Rs 2,00,600. What must he reverse?
completion:
He must reverse Rs 30,600 of input tax credit (ITC). The 180 days from 1 February 2026 ended on 31 July 2026, and half of the invoice was still unpaid.
Invoice total = 3,40,000 + 61,200 = Rs 4,01,200.
Unpaid = 4,01,200 - 2,00,600 = Rs 2,00,600, which is 50%.
Reversal = 50% x 61,200 = Rs 30,600.
Add it to output tax in the GSTR-3B for August 2026, the period after the 180 days, together with interest under Section 50. When he pays the balance, he re-claims the Rs 30,600. Reference: Rule 37 of the CGST Rules and the second proviso to Section 16(2) of the CGST Act.

prompt: Invoice dated 2 December 2025 for Rs 1,77,000 including GST of Rs 27,000. We paid Rs 1,18,000 on 10 January and nothing more by 31 May 2026. How much ITC goes back?
completion:
Reverse Rs 9,000 of input tax credit (ITC), the share of tax in the unpaid one-third of the invoice.
Unpaid = 1,77,000 - 1,18,000 = Rs 59,000.
Unpaid share = 59,000 / 1,77,000 = 1/3.
Reversal = 1/3 x 27,000 = Rs 9,000.
The 180 days from 2 December 2025 ended on 31 May 2026, so show Rs 9,000 in the GSTR-3B for June 2026. The Rs 18,000 on the paid portion stays. Paying the Rs 59,000 later lets you re-claim the Rs 9,000 in that month's return. Reference: Rule 37 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: A supplier in Kolhapur, Maharashtra, charged us CGST+SGST of Rs 72,000 on goods delivered to our Belagavi, Karnataka unit, billed on our Karnataka GSTIN. Can we claim it?
completion: No. Do not claim the Rs 72,000. The supply is inter-state, Maharashtra to Karnataka, so integrated GST (IGST) is due, and Maharashtra's central GST (CGST) and state GST (SGST) cannot be claimed by a Karnataka GSTIN. Ask the supplier to issue a credit note cancelling the wrong tax and a fresh invoice charging IGST of Rs 72,000. You claim the IGST once it reaches your GSTR-2B. The supplier pays the correct IGST first, owes no interest on it, and then claims a refund of the CGST and SGST wrongly paid. Reference: Section 77(1) of the CGST Act and Section 19(2) of the IGST Act, 2017.

prompt: We charged IGST of Rs 1,26,000 on a sale within Telangana that should have been CGST+SGST. Do we pay interest when we correct it?
completion: No interest is payable on the correct tax. Pay central GST (CGST) of Rs 63,000 and state GST (SGST) of Rs 63,000, which together equal the Rs 1,26,000 integrated GST (IGST) charged in error. Then claim a refund of the Rs 1,26,000 IGST wrongly paid. The law treats this as tax paid under the wrong head, not as late payment. Issue a credit note for the IGST invoice and a fresh invoice with CGST and SGST, so the buyer's credit is also corrected. Reference: Section 77(2) of the CGST Act and Section 19(1) of the IGST Act, 2017.

prompt:
User: Is a works contract for building a warehouse a composite supply?
Assistant: Yes; the law treats it as a supply of services.
User: The contract is Rs 1,20,00,000, partly materials. Can the builder charge 18% on labour and a lower rate on cement?
completion:
No. A works contract for immovable property is treated as a single supply of services, so one rate applies to the full value, not item-wise rates for materials and labour. For a commercial warehouse the rate is 18%.
GST 1,20,00,000 x 18% = Rs 21,60,000.
Contract total = Rs 1,41,60,000.
The builder can claim input tax credit (ITC) on the materials and services it uses. The warehouse owner cannot claim ITC on the contract, because works contract services for construction of its own immovable property are blocked. Reference: Section 2(119), Schedule II para 6(a) and Section 17(5)(c) of the CGST Act.

prompt: Besides salary, a whole-time director receives a commission of Rs 9,00,000, booked as professional fees with income-tax TDS deducted as fees, not as salary. Is GST due?
completion:
Yes. The company pays GST of Rs 1,62,000 under reverse charge on the commission. CBIC treats a director's pay according to how it is booked. Amounts treated as salary, with salary tax deduction, are outside GST. Amounts booked as fees for professional services, with tax deducted as fees, are a supply by the director to the company and fall under the reverse charge mechanism (RCM).
Tax = 9,00,000 x 18% = Rs 1,62,000.
Pay it in cash; claim it as input tax credit (ITC) if the company uses the service for taxable supplies. If the commission were paid as salary, no GST would arise. Reference: CBIC Circular 140/10/2020-GST and Notification 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), entry 6.

prompt: Our aggregate turnover last year was Rs 12 crore. An invoice dated 2 October 2026 was sent to the IRP on 6 November 2026. Accepted?
completion: No. The invoice registration portal (IRP) will reject it. Taxpayers with aggregate turnover of Rs 10 crore or more cannot report an invoice older than 30 days from the reporting date. From 2 October to 6 November is 35 days. Without an invoice reference number (IRN), the document is not a valid tax invoice, and the buyer cannot claim input tax credit (ITC). The 30-day limit has applied to this turnover band since 1 April 2025. It covers invoices, credit notes and debit notes. Reference: Rule 48(4) and Rule 48(5) of the CGST Rules and the GSTN advisory on the reporting time limit.

prompt: A company with turnover of Rs 8 crore reports an invoice to the IRP 40 days after the invoice date. Will the IRP reject it?
completion: No. The 30-day reporting limit applies only to taxpayers with aggregate turnover of Rs 10 crore or more, and this company is below that band, so the invoice registration portal (IRP) will not reject the invoice for being 40 days old. It is still bound by e-invoicing, because its turnover exceeds Rs 5 crore, so every B2B invoice needs an invoice reference number (IRN). Without an IRN the document is not a valid tax invoice. Generate the IRN on the invoice date as routine rather than relying on the absence of a limit. Reference: Rule 48(4) of the CGST Rules and the GSTN advisory on the reporting time limit.

prompt: A cement stockist in Guntur sells cement worth Rs 3,20,000. What GST, and was it different before September 2025?
completion:
Charge 18% GST: Rs 57,600. Cement moved from 28% to 18% on 22 September 2025.
Value 3,20,000 x 18% = Rs 57,600.
Invoice total = Rs 3,77,600.
Under the old 28% rate the tax would have been Rs 89,600, so the change saves Rs 32,000 on this sale. Stock bought before the change and sold after it carries the new rate on the sale. The rate on the purchase does not matter. Reference: GST 2.0 rate schedule for cement, effective 22 September 2025.

prompt: Is GST charged on a family floater health insurance policy taken by an individual, and on a group policy taken by an employer?
completion: No GST on the individual family floater policy; 18% on the employer's group policy. From 22 September 2025, individual health insurance and individual life insurance policies, including family floaters and policies for senior citizens, are exempt from GST. Group policies bought by an employer are still taxed at 18%. For example, a group premium of Rs 7,40,000 carries GST of 7,40,000 x 18% = Rs 1,33,200. Reference: Notification 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate), effective 22 September 2025, and the Department of Financial Services GST FAQ on insurance.

prompt:
User: Our manufacturing company in Ludhiana took design consultancy from a UK firm.
Assistant: That is an import of services taxed under reverse charge.
User: Fee is Rs 6,50,000. How much tax, which head, and can we take credit?
completion:
Pay integrated GST (IGST) of Rs 1,17,000 under reverse charge, and claim the same amount as credit. An import of services is an inter-state supply, so the tax is always IGST.
Tax = 6,50,000 x 18% = Rs 1,17,000.
Pay it in cash and report it in Table 3.1(d) of GSTR-3B. Claim it as input tax credit (ITC) in Table 4(A)(2) in the same return, since the consultancy is used for your taxable business. Reference: Section 5(3) of the IGST Act, 2017 and Notification 10/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate).

prompt: A restaurant in Puducherry under composition has a quarter turnover of Rs 18,40,000. What tax does it pay?
completion:
It pays composition tax of Rs 92,000 for the quarter, at 5% of turnover for restaurants not serving alcohol.
Tax 18,40,000 x 5% = Rs 92,000, split central GST (CGST) Rs 46,000 and state GST (SGST) Rs 46,000. Puducherry has its own legislature, so it levies SGST, not Union territory GST (UTGST).
Pay through Form CMP-08 by the 18th of the month after the quarter. The restaurant cannot collect tax from customers or claim input tax credit (ITC). A manufacturer or trader would pay 1%, and a service provider under the services scheme 6%. Reference: Section 10 of the CGST Act and Rule 7 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: Our turnover crossed Rs 5 crore in December 2026 for the first time. When must we start e-invoicing?
completion: Start e-invoicing from 1 April 2027. E-invoicing applies to a taxpayer whose aggregate turnover exceeded Rs 5 crore in any preceding financial year from 2017-18. Crossing the limit during 2026-27 brings you in from the start of the next year, not immediately. Invoices issued in January to March 2027 need no invoice reference number (IRN). From April 2027 every business-to-business invoice, export invoice, credit note and debit note needs an IRN. Once in, you stay in even if turnover later falls below Rs 5 crore. Reference: Rule 48(4) of the CGST Rules and Notification 10/2023-Central Tax.

prompt: An NBFC in Chennai has turnover of Rs 220 crore. Must it issue e-invoices?
completion: No. A non-banking financial company (NBFC) is exempt from e-invoicing whatever its turnover. Notification 13/2020-Central Tax exempts insurers, banking companies and financial institutions including NBFCs, and later notifications added goods transport agencies (GTA), passenger transport operators, multiplex cinema admissions and special economic zone (SEZ) units. The NBFC therefore issues normal tax invoices under Rule 46 from its own system, with no invoice reference number (IRN) from the portal, and reports them in GSTR-1. Its turnover of Rs 220 crore does not change this. Reference: Notification 13/2020-Central Tax, as amended, and Rule 46 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: An online marketplace's seller in Jaipur had supplies of Rs 18,60,000 and returns of Rs 1,10,000 this month. What TCS does the operator collect?
completion:
The operator collects tax collected at source (TCS) of Rs 8,750, at 0.5% of net taxable supplies.
Net = 18,60,000 - 1,10,000 = Rs 17,50,000.
TCS = 17,50,000 x 0.5% = Rs 8,750, split central GST (CGST) Rs 4,375 and state GST (SGST) Rs 4,375 for intra-state sales.
The rate has been 0.5% since 10 July 2024. The operator reports it in GSTR-8. The seller accepts it and uses it from the electronic cash ledger. Reference: Section 52 of the CGST Act and Notification 15/2024-Central Tax.

prompt: Hotel room tariff is exactly Rs 7,500 a night in Shimla; another room is Rs 7,501. GST on each?
completion:
Charge 5% without input tax credit (ITC) on the Rs 7,500 room, and 18% with ITC on the Rs 7,501 room. Accommodation up to Rs 7,500 per unit per day takes 5% after GST 2.0, so one rupee more moves the room to 18%.
Rs 7,500 x 5% = Rs 375.
Rs 7,501 x 18% = Rs 1,350.18.
The threshold is tested per room unit and per day, not on the hotel's star rating or the invoice total. A hotel charging up to Rs 7,500 cannot opt for the 18% slab with ITC. Reference: GST 2.0 rate schedule for accommodation services, effective 22 September 2025.

prompt: A spice trader in Kozhikode with Rs 1.2 crore turnover last year files his GSTR-3B 23 days late, with tax payable. Late fee?
completion:
The late fee is Rs 1,150: Rs 575 central GST (CGST) and Rs 575 state GST (SGST). For a return with tax liability the fee is Rs 50 a day, Rs 25 under each act. For aggregate turnover up to Rs 1.5 crore it is capped at Rs 2,000 per return.
23 days x Rs 50 = Rs 1,150.
The cap is not reached. Pay it in cash only. Interest at 18% a year on the late tax is a separate charge under Section 50(1). Reference: Section 47 of the CGST Act and Notification 19/2021-Central Tax.

prompt: A company wrongly availed ITC of Rs 80,000 on 20 August 2026, and the ledger balance fell below that amount on the same day. It reversed it on 30 October 2026. Interest?
completion:
Interest is Rs 2,801 at 18% a year. Wrongly availed input tax credit (ITC) attracts interest once it is utilised. Utilisation is taken from the date the credit ledger balance falls below the wrong amount.
Days: 21 to 31 August = 11, September = 30, 1 to 30 October = 30, total 71 days.
Interest = 80,000 x 18% x 71 / 365 = Rs 2,801.10, rounded to Rs 2,801.
Pay it in cash through Form DRC-03 or the GSTR-3B interest field. Reference: Section 50(3) of the CGST Act, Notification 14/2022-Central Tax and Rule 88B of the CGST Rules.

prompt: A March 2026 invoice in our GSTR-1 shows the buyer's wrong GSTIN. Until when can we amend it?
completion: Amend it by 30 November 2026, which is days away. A GSTR-1 detail for financial year 2025-26 can be rectified only until 30 November 2026 or the date of filing the annual return for 2025-26, whichever is earlier. Report the corrected buyer GSTIN through the amendment tables of a GSTR-1 for a current period, and do it now rather than on the last day. After that date the GSTR-1 entry for that invoice can no longer be rectified. Reference: proviso to Section 37(3) of the CGST Act.

prompt: we sell online to customers in many states, unregistered. which table in 3b?
completion: Report them in Table 3.1(a) for tax, and also state-wise in Table 3.2. Inter-state supplies to unregistered persons are taxable outward supplies, so the value and integrated GST (IGST) go in Table 3.1(a). Table 3.2 then breaks the same figures down by place of supply for each state. For example, Rs 1,80,000 to customers in Bihar at 18% shows IGST of Rs 32,400 against Bihar in Table 3.2. These values are auto-filled from GSTR-1, so report the place of supply correctly there. Reference: Rule 61 of the CGST Rules and Section 10 of the IGST Act, 2017.

prompt: A design firm in Bhopal finished a project on 5 August 2026, invoiced on 20 August and was paid on 10 September. What is the time of supply?
completion:
The time of supply is 20 August 2026, the invoice date. The invoice was issued within the 30 days allowed for services, so the time of supply is the earlier of the invoice date and the payment date, 10 September.
Report the tax in the August 2026 GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B.
If the client had paid an advance before 20 August, the advance date would have been the time of supply for that amount. Reference: Section 13(2)(a) of the CGST Act and Rule 47 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: An HR consultant in Nagpur completed an assignment on 5 August 2026 but invoiced only on 25 September and was paid on 30 September. Which month's return carries the tax?
completion:
The tax belongs in the August 2026 return, not September. The invoice came more than 30 days after the service was provided, so the time of supply becomes the earlier of the date of provision, 5 August, and the payment date.
If the tax was paid only with the September return on 20 October, interest runs from 21 September. On a fee of Rs 3,50,000 at 18%, tax is Rs 63,000. For 30 days, interest = 63,000 x 18% x 30 / 365 = Rs 932.05, rounded to Rs 932. Reference: Section 13(2)(b) of the CGST Act and Rule 47 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: A bank in Mumbai provided advisory services completed on 10 September 2026 and invoiced on 20 October. Is the invoice late?
completion: No. A bank has 45 days from the date of supply to issue a service invoice, not 30. 10 September to 20 October is 40 days, within that limit. The time of supply is therefore the invoice date, 20 October 2026, or the payment date if earlier. The extended 45-day period applies to banking companies, insurers and financial institutions including non-banking financial companies (NBFCs). A non-financial firm invoicing on the 40th day would be late. Reference: proviso to Rule 47 of the CGST Rules and Section 13(2) of the CGST Act.

prompt:
User: An architect in Bengaluru received an advance of Rs 2,36,000 including tax on 12 July 2026.
Assistant: For services, GST is due on advances.
User: The work was done on 30 August and the final bill is Rs 7,08,000 including tax. How is tax split between months?
completion:
Pay Rs 36,000 in July on the advance, and Rs 72,000 on the balance, assuming 18% GST, that Rs 7,08,000 is the total bill including the advance, and that the invoice is issued in August within 30 days of completion.
Advance tax = 2,36,000 x 18/118 = Rs 36,000, in the July 2026 return, with a receipt voucher.
Total tax on the bill = 7,08,000 x 18/118 = Rs 1,08,000.
Balance tax = 1,08,000 - 36,000 = Rs 72,000.
The invoice shows the full value and adjusts the advance already taxed. Reference: Section 13(2) of the CGST Act and Rule 50 of the CGST Rules.

prompt:
User: A company receives legal services under reverse charge.
Assistant: Time of supply under reverse charge follows special rules.
User: Invoice dated 1 August 2026, paid on 20 November 2026. Which month is the tax due?
completion:
The tax is due for October 2026, not November. For services under reverse charge, the time of supply is the earlier of the payment date and the day immediately following 60 days from the invoice date.
60 days from 1 August ends on 30 September, so the following day is 1 October 2026.
The payment on 20 November is later, so 1 October wins.
Pay the reverse charge tax in the October 2026 GSTR-3B. Paying it in November adds interest under Section 50(1) from 21 November. Reference: Section 13(3) of the CGST Act.

prompt: Is there a time limit for a debit note for under-charged tax on a June 2025 invoice?
completion: No. Section 34 sets no time limit for issuing a debit note, unlike a credit note, which has the 30 November cut-off under Section 34(2). A debit note for under-charged tax on a June 2025 invoice can therefore be issued now. The supplier declares it in the GSTR-1 for the month of issue and pays the extra tax. Reference: Section 34 of the CGST Act.

prompt:
User: We file GSTR-1 monthly; our turnover is Rs 2 crore.
Assistant: The due date is the 11th of the next month.
User: What if a month has no sales at all? Do we still file, and what is the late fee if we forget for a month?
completion:
Yes. File a nil GSTR-1 even when there are no sales. If you forget, the late fee for a nil GSTR-1 is Rs 20 a day, Rs 10 central GST (CGST) and Rs 10 state GST (SGST), capped at Rs 500 per return (Rs 250 + Rs 250).
Forgetting for 30 days: 30 x Rs 20 = Rs 600, capped at Rs 500.
A nil GSTR-1 can also be filed by SMS to 14409, but only if no data is saved on the portal for that period. Reference: Section 37 and Section 47 of the CGST Act and Notification 20/2021-Central Tax.

prompt: For July 2026 wages, an employee's basic + DA is Rs 22,000 and the employer restricts PF to the ceiling. Split the employer's 12% between EPS and EPF.
completion:
The employer pays Rs 1,800, split Rs 1,250 to the pension scheme (EPS) and Rs 550 to the provident fund (EPF). For July 2026 the wage ceiling was Rs 15,000.
Employee share: 15,000 x 12% = Rs 1,800.
Employer share: 15,000 x 12% = Rs 1,800.
EPS: 15,000 x 8.33% = Rs 1,249.50, rounded to Rs 1,250.
EPF (employer): 1,800 - 1,250 = Rs 550, about 3.67%.
The employer also pays EDLI at 0.5% of Rs 15,000 = Rs 75, and admin charges at 0.5% of Rs 15,000 = Rs 75. Reference: EPFO contribution rates (12% employer share, 8.33% to EPS, 3.67% to EPF).

prompt: PF wages of Rs 12,400 for June 2026. What does each party pay into EPF and EPS?
completion:
The employee pays Rs 1,488. The employer pays Rs 1,488, split Rs 1,033 to the pension scheme (EPS) and Rs 455 to the provident fund (EPF). The wage is below the Rs 15,000 ceiling, so contributions are on the actual wage.
Employee: 12,400 x 12% = Rs 1,488.
EPS: 12,400 x 8.33% = Rs 1,032.92, rounded to Rs 1,033.
Employer EPF: 1,488 - 1,033 = Rs 455.
EDLI at 0.5% = Rs 62. Reference: EPFO contribution rates (12% each, employer share 8.33% to EPS, rest to EPF).

prompt: what is employer total pf cost on 15000 basic incl edli admin, for may 2026
completion:
The employer's total PF cost is Rs 1,950 for May 2026.
Employer contribution: 15,000 x 12% = Rs 1,800 (pension scheme, EPS, Rs 1,250 and provident fund, EPF, Rs 550).
Employees' deposit-linked insurance (EDLI): 15,000 x 0.5% = Rs 75.
Administrative charges: 15,000 x 0.5% = Rs 75.
Total = 1,800 + 75 + 75 = Rs 1,950.
The employee's Rs 1,800 is deducted from salary, so it is not an employer cost. Admin charges have a minimum of Rs 500 per establishment per month. Reference: EPFO contribution rates (employer 12%, EDLI 0.5%, admin 0.5%).

prompt: old regime 2025-26, salary 6.4 lakh, 80c 1.5 lakh done, mediclaim 25k. any tax?
completion:
No. Tax is nil after the rebate.
Taxable = 6,40,000 - 50,000 standard deduction - 1,50,000 (Section 80C) - 25,000 (Section 80D) = Rs 4,15,000.
Slab tax: 2.5-4.15 lakh = 1,65,000 x 5% = Rs 8,250.
Rebate under Section 87A, for income up to Rs 5 lakh, is up to Rs 12,500, so the Rs 8,250 is wiped out.
Tax = Rs 0, and no tax deducted at source (TDS) under Section 192 is needed if proofs are submitted. Reference: Income-tax Act, 1961, for financial year 2025-26.

prompt: At what taxable income does marginal relief stop in the new regime? Check Rs 12,75,000.
completion:
Marginal relief stops at a taxable income of about Rs 12,70,588. At Rs 12,75,000 no relief is available.
Slab tax at Rs 12,75,000 = 60,000 + 75,000 x 15% = Rs 71,250.
Income above Rs 12 lakh = Rs 75,000, which is more than Rs 71,250, so no cap applies.
Tax = 71,250 + 4% cess 2,850 = Rs 74,100.
Break-even: 60,000 + 15% of x = x gives x = Rs 70,588, so relief applies up to a taxable income of about Rs 12,70,588. Reference: Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 87A for 2025-26).

prompt:
User: My taxable income is Rs 12 lakh, so no tax.
Assistant: Yes, the rebate covers it fully in the new regime.
User: My employer added a Rs 5,000 reward in March, so taxable income is Rs 12,05,000. Do I now pay Rs 63,000?
completion:
No. You pay Rs 5,200, thanks to marginal relief.
Slab tax on Rs 12,05,000 = 60,000 + 5,000 x 15% = Rs 60,750.
Marginal relief caps tax at the income above Rs 12 lakh = Rs 5,000.
Tax = 5,000 + 4% cess 200 = Rs 5,200.
Your employer should deduct this Rs 5,200 in March under Section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Without relief the figure would have been Rs 63,180. Reference: Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

prompt: FY 2025-26, old regime: basic Rs 45,000 a month, HRA Rs 22,500 a month, rent Rs 25,000 a month in Chennai. Compute HRA exemption.
completion:
The house rent allowance (HRA) exemption is Rs 2,46,000, so Rs 24,000 of HRA is taxable. The exemption is the least of three amounts:
1. Actual HRA = 22,500 x 12 = Rs 2,70,000.
2. Rent minus 10% of salary = 3,00,000 - 54,000 = Rs 2,46,000, where salary = 45,000 x 12 = Rs 5,40,000.
3. 50% of salary, as Chennai is a metro = Rs 2,70,000.
Least = Rs 2,46,000. Taxable HRA = 2,70,000 - 2,46,000 = Rs 24,000.
In the new regime the full Rs 2,70,000 is taxable. Reference: Section 10(13A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Rule 2A.

prompt: Employee in Pune, old regime FY 2025-26: basic Rs 50,000 a month, HRA Rs 20,000 a month, rent Rs 18,000 a month. He used 50% as metro. Correct?
completion:
No. Pune is not a metro for house rent allowance (HRA), so the limit is 40%. The exemption is Rs 1,56,000 either way, because the rent test is lowest.
1. Actual HRA = Rs 2,40,000.
2. Rent - 10% of salary = 2,16,000 - 60,000 = Rs 1,56,000.
3. 40% of salary = 6,00,000 x 40% = Rs 2,40,000.
Exempt = Rs 1,56,000; taxable HRA = Rs 84,000.
For financial year 2025-26, only Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai get 50%. Reference: Section 10(13A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Rule 2A.

prompt: An employee lives in a flat he owns in Lucknow and receives HRA. Can he claim HRA exemption?
completion: No. House rent allowance (HRA) exemption needs rent actually paid for accommodation he occupies. Living in his own flat, he pays no rent, so the whole HRA is taxable. For example, HRA of Rs 15,000 a month adds Rs 1,80,000 to taxable salary. In the old regime he may instead claim interest on a home loan for that flat, up to Rs 2,00,000 under Section 24(b). In the new regime that interest deduction is not allowed for a self-occupied house. Reference: Section 10(13A) and Section 24(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, for financial year 2025-26.

prompt: Can the employer give Section 89 arrears relief while deducting TDS, or must the employee claim it in the return?
completion: The employer can give it while computing tax deducted at source (TDS). An employee who receives arrears can apply to the employer, and the employer then reduces TDS by the relief, computed as in Rule 21A. The employee must still file Form 10E on the portal before the return, or the claim is questioned. For financial year 2025-26 this is Sections 89 and 192(2A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. From tax year 2026-27, the relief is under Section 157 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 39 replacing Form 10E. Reference: Section 192(2A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: Two employers in FY 2025-26 both allowed the Rs 75,000 standard deduction and both deducted nil TDS. What goes wrong?
completion: The employee ends up owing tax at filing, because only one standard deduction of Rs 75,000 is allowed in a year. For example, salaries of Rs 6,50,000 and Rs 6,40,000 each look tax-free on their own. Combined, the salary is Rs 12,90,000 and taxable income is Rs 12,15,000. Slab tax is Rs 62,250, and marginal relief caps it at Rs 15,000, so tax with cess is Rs 15,600. The employee pays this as self-assessment tax with interest under Sections 234B and 234C if applicable. Giving Form 12B to the second employer avoids this. Reference: Section 16(ia) and Section 192(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: When are the Form 24Q returns and Form 16 due for FY 2025-26?
completion:
Form 24Q, the quarterly statement of salary tax deducted at source (TDS), is due on:
Q1 (April-June): 31 July 2025.
Q2 (July-September): 31 October 2025.
Q3 (October-December): 31 January 2026.
Q4 (January-March): 31 May 2026.
Form 16 must be issued by 15 June 2026.
From tax year 2026-27, the quarterly statement is Form 138 and the certificate is Form 130 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Reference: Rule 31A and Rule 31 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, for financial year 2025-26.

prompt: TDS of Rs 48,000 was deducted from salary on 30 April 2025 but deposited on 12 June 2025. What interest is due?
completion:
Interest is Rs 1,440, at 1.5% for each month or part month from deduction to deposit.
30 April to 29 May = 1 month; 30 May to 12 June = part of a second month. Total = 2 months.
Interest = 48,000 x 1.5% x 2 = Rs 1,440.
Pay it with the tax deducted at source (TDS) through challan before filing Form 24Q. If TDS had not been deducted at all, interest would be 1% a month from the date it should have been deducted. Reference: Section 201(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, for financial year 2025-26.

prompt: Old regime FY 2025-26: employee PF Rs 72,000, PPF Rs 50,000, life insurance premium Rs 40,000, children's tuition fees Rs 36,000. How much 80C?
completion:
The Section 80C deduction is Rs 1,50,000, the cap, although investments total Rs 1,98,000.
Total = 72,000 + 50,000 + 40,000 + 36,000 = Rs 1,98,000.
Allowed = Rs 1,50,000.
The extra Rs 48,000 gives no further deduction. All four items qualify under Section 80C. Employee PF counts automatically through payroll. Ask for proofs of the PPF, insurance and tuition fees by the employer's cut-off date. In the new regime none of these is deductible. Reference: Section 80C of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: An employee aged 62 in Nashik, old regime FY 2025-26, has salary Rs 8,50,000 and no deductions. Tax?
completion:
Tax is Rs 72,800. A resident senior citizen aged 60 to 80 has a basic exemption of Rs 3,00,000 under the old regime.
Taxable = 8,50,000 - 50,000 = Rs 8,00,000.
0-3 lakh: nil.
3-5 lakh: 2,00,000 x 5% = Rs 10,000.
5-8 lakh: 3,00,000 x 20% = Rs 60,000.
Slab tax = Rs 70,000; cess Rs 2,800; total Rs 72,800.
In the new regime, his taxable income of Rs 7,75,000 would give nil tax after the rebate, so the new regime saves him Rs 72,800. Reference: Section 115BAC and the First Schedule to the Finance Act, 2025.

prompt: FY 2025-26: tax computed is Rs 62,400 for the year. From April to December the employer deducted Rs 36,000. What must be deducted in Jan-Mar?
completion:
Deduct Rs 26,400 in total, Rs 8,800 a month, from January to March.
Balance = 62,400 - 36,000 = Rs 26,400.
Monthly = 26,400 / 3 = Rs 8,800.
The employer must deduct the full annual tax by March. Any shortfall at year end is a default, with interest at 1% a month and possible penalty. Recompute in January using the employee's final proof of investments before fixing the figure. Reference: Section 192 and Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: A pensioner of 81 years with pension Rs 9,40,000 in FY 2025-26, old regime. Tax?
completion:
Tax is Rs 81,120, even after the higher exemption for very senior citizens. A resident aged 80 or above has a basic exemption of Rs 5,00,000 under the old regime.
Taxable = 9,40,000 - 50,000 standard deduction = Rs 8,90,000.
0-5 lakh: nil.
5-8.9 lakh: 3,90,000 x 20% = Rs 78,000.
Slab tax = Rs 78,000; cess Rs 3,120; total Rs 81,120.
In the new regime, taxable income of Rs 8,65,000 gives nil tax after the rebate, so the new regime saves Rs 81,120. Reference: Section 115BAC and Section 16(ia) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: An employee on Rs 1,60,000 a month leaves on 30 September 2026. FnF has leave encashment Rs 1,20,000 (fully exempt) and gratuity Rs 2,70,000 (fully exempt). New regime. What TDS?
completion:
Tax deducted at source (TDS) for the year is nil.
Taxable salary April-September = 6 x 1,60,000 = Rs 9,60,000.
Leave encashment and gratuity are exempt, so they add nothing.
Taxable income = 9,60,000 - 75,000 = Rs 8,85,000; slab tax Rs 28,500, fully rebated under Section 156.
If the employer deducted TDS on an annual projection of Rs 19,20,000, it over-deducted. Stop deductions in the FnF month, and the employee claims a refund in the return. Report the figures in the Q1 and Q2 Form 138. Reference: Section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

prompt: An employee who left in August 2025 asks when she will get Form 16 from us.
completion: Issue Form 16 by 15 June 2026, for the period April to August 2025. Form 16 is an annual certificate issued after the financial year ends and after the Q4 Form 24Q is filed. Part A, downloaded from TRACES, shows tax deducted at source (TDS) deposited. Part B shows the salary computation for the months worked. Give her a salary and tax statement at exit, so her next employer can account for this income. For exits in tax year 2026-27 and later, the certificate is Form 130 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Reference: Rule 31 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and Section 203 of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: An NBFC in Mumbai completed loan-processing services on 2 August 2026 and invoiced on 10 September. Is the invoice late?
completion: No. A non-banking financial company (NBFC) has 45 days from the date of supply to issue a service invoice, not 30. From 2 August to 10 September is 39 days, within that limit. The time of supply is therefore the invoice date, 10 September 2026, unless payment came earlier. Report it in the September 2026 return. For example, a fee of Rs 1,80,000 carries GST of 1,80,000 x 18% = Rs 32,400, due by 20 October. Reference: proviso to Rule 47 of the CGST Rules and Section 13(2) of the CGST Act.

prompt:
User: A printing press in Vijayawada finished a job on 8 September and invoiced it on 29 September.
Assistant: The invoice was within 30 days, so the time of supply is the invoice date.
User: The customer had paid Rs 40,000 advance on 1 September. Does that change anything?
completion: Yes, for the advance. The Rs 40,000 received on 1 September has its own time of supply, the payment date, because for services the time of supply is the earlier of invoice and payment. If the advance includes tax at 18%, the tax on it is 40,000 x 18/118 = Rs 6,101.69, due in the September 2026 return. Here both dates are in September, so the return period does not change, but issue a receipt voucher for the advance. The balance is taxed on the 29 September invoice. Reference: Section 13(2)(a) of the CGST Act and Rule 50 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: A consultant in Mohali became liable to register on 5 August 2026, applied on 20 August and got registration on 1 September. What about invoices issued in August without GST?
completion: Issue revised tax invoices for supplies made between 5 August and 31 August by 1 October 2026. Registration is effective from 5 August, the date of liability, because she applied within 30 days. Revised invoices for that period must be issued within one month of the date of the registration certificate, 1 September. For example, if fees of Rs 1,60,000 billed in August excluded tax, GST at 18% is 1,60,000 x 18% = Rs 28,800, payable on those supplies. Reference: Section 31(3)(a) of the CGST Act and Rule 53 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: We billed an item at 5% GST, Rs 2,40,000 taxable value, but its correct rate is 18%. How do we fix it?
completion:
Issue a debit note for the under-charged tax of Rs 31,200.
Tax charged = 2,40,000 x 5% = Rs 12,000.
Correct tax = 2,40,000 x 18% = Rs 43,200.
Shortfall = 43,200 - 12,000 = Rs 31,200.
The debit note refers to the original invoice and shows the extra tax of Rs 31,200. Report it in GSTR-1 for the month of issue and pay the tax. The buyer can claim the Rs 31,200 as input tax credit (ITC), subject to the usual conditions. Reference: Section 34 of the CGST Act and Rule 53 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: What details must a GST credit note contain, and when can it be issued?
completion: A credit note must carry the supplier's name, address and GSTIN, the words 'Credit Note', a consecutive serial number, the date, the recipient's details, the number and date of the original invoice, the taxable value, tax rate and tax amount credited, and a signature. It can be issued when the taxable value or tax charged was too high, when goods are returned, or when goods or services were found deficient. For a supply in financial year 2025-26, it must be declared in the return by 30 November 2026, or the annual return date if earlier. For example, a credit note for Rs 12,000 plus Rs 2,160 GST (18%) reduces output tax by Rs 2,160. Reference: Section 34(1) and Section 34(2) of the CGST Act and Rule 53 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: An event agency in Udupi got an advance of Rs 59,000 including 18% GST in September 2026. The final bill in November is Rs 2,36,000 including GST. Show the tax and balance.
completion:
Tax of Rs 9,000 was paid in September, Rs 27,000 is due in November, and the balance receivable is Rs 1,77,000.
Advance: 59,000 x 18 / 118 = Rs 9,000 tax; base Rs 50,000.
Final: 2,36,000 x 18 / 118 = Rs 36,000 tax; base Rs 2,00,000.
November tax = 36,000 - 9,000 = Rs 27,000.
Balance due from the client = 2,36,000 - 59,000 = Rs 1,77,000.
The November invoice shows the full value and tax, then deducts the advance and its tax. Reference: Section 13(2) of the CGST Act and Rule 50 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: Invoice dated 4 March 2026: Rs 6,50,000 + 18% GST. The buyer paid Rs 4,60,200 by 31 August 2026 and nothing more. ITC reversal under Rule 37?
completion:
Reverse input tax credit (ITC) of Rs 46,800, because 40% of the invoice was still unpaid after 180 days.
The 180 days from 4 March 2026 ended on 31 August 2026.
Invoice total = 6,50,000 + 1,17,000 = Rs 7,67,000.
Paid = Rs 4,60,200 (60%); unpaid = Rs 3,06,800 (40%).
Reversal = 40% x 1,17,000 = Rs 46,800.
Add it to output tax in the September 2026 GSTR-3B, with interest at 18% if the credit was used. Re-claim it when the balance is paid. Reference: Rule 37 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: A textile buyer in Bhilwara had invoice of 4 May 2026 for Rs 2,80,000 + 5% GST, paid Rs 1,47,000 by 31 October 2026 and the balance on 18 December 2026. Show the reversal and re-claim.
completion:
Reverse Rs 7,000 in November 2026 and re-claim Rs 7,000 in December 2026.
180 days from 4 May 2026 ended on 31 October 2026.
Invoice total = 2,80,000 + 14,000 = Rs 2,94,000.
Unpaid on 31 October = 2,94,000 - 1,47,000 = Rs 1,47,000, which is 50%.
Reversal = 50% x 14,000 = Rs 7,000, in the November 2026 GSTR-3B.
Balance paid on 18 December, so re-claim Rs 7,000 in the December 2026 GSTR-3B. Interest applies for the period if the credit had been used. Reference: Rule 37 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: FY 2025-26: a company in Patiala pays a lawyer Rs 80,000 plus GST Rs 14,400. What TDS and what net payment?
completion:
Deduct tax deducted at source (TDS) of Rs 8,000 and pay the lawyer Rs 86,400. Professional fees attract TDS at 10% under Section 194J of the Income-tax Act, 1961, once fees in the year exceed Rs 50,000. TDS is on the fee excluding GST, when GST is shown separately.
TDS = 80,000 x 10% = Rs 8,000.
Invoice total = 80,000 + 14,400 = Rs 94,400.
Net payment = 94,400 - 8,000 = Rs 86,400.
Deposit TDS by the 7th of the next month, file Form 26Q, and issue Form 16A. Reference: Section 194J and CBDT Circular 23/2017.

prompt: FY 2025-26: an engineering firm pays Rs 3,00,000 plus GST for technical services (not professional). What TDS rate?
completion:
Deduct tax deducted at source (TDS) at 2%, Rs 6,000. Fees for technical services carry 2%, while professional services carry 10%.
GST = 3,00,000 x 18% = Rs 54,000.
Invoice total = Rs 3,54,000.
TDS = 3,00,000 x 2% = Rs 6,000.
Net payment = 3,54,000 - 6,000 = Rs 3,48,000.
If the work was professional services, such as legal or engineering consultancy by a professional, TDS would be Rs 30,000. Classify from the contract, not the invoice title. Reference: Section 194J(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: Under an April 2026 agreement, a distributor in Moradabad earns a 2% volume discount linked to invoices. August 2026 purchases were Rs 12,50,000 at 18%. Credit note?
completion:
Issue a credit note of Rs 29,500 with GST. The discount was agreed before supply (April 2026) and linked to the August invoices, so it can be excluded from the value of supply under Section 15(3)(b) whichever version of the rule applies.
Discount = 12,50,000 x 2% = Rs 25,000.
GST = 25,000 x 18% = Rs 4,500.
Credit note total = Rs 29,500.
Revised value of August purchases = Rs 12,25,000.
List the linked invoice numbers on the credit note. Reference: Section 15(3)(b) and Section 34 of the CGST Act.

prompt: A seller in Sikar issued an invoice for goods at 5% (Rs 1,20,000) and a second line at 18% (Rs 50,000). The buyer returns half of the 18% goods. Credit note?
completion:
Issue a credit note for Rs 29,500 against the 18% line only.
Returned value = 50,000 x 50% = Rs 25,000.
GST 18% = Rs 4,500.
Credit note = Rs 29,500.
The 5% line stays untouched.
Revised invoice: 5% line Rs 1,20,000 + Rs 6,000; 18% line Rs 25,000 + Rs 4,500.
Show the original invoice number and the line returned on the credit note. Reference: Section 34(1) of the CGST Act.

prompt: A furniture maker in Tirunelveli receives Rs 2,00,000 advance in October 2026 for goods to be delivered in January 2027 at 18%. How do the October and January documents look?
completion:
In October issue a receipt voucher with no GST. In January issue the full invoice with GST of Rs 63,000, and adjust the advance.
GST is not due on advances for goods, so October shows no tax.
January invoice, if the full price is Rs 3,50,000: GST 18% = Rs 63,000; total Rs 4,13,000.
Less advance received Rs 2,00,000; balance due Rs 2,13,000.
The whole Rs 63,000 is paid in the January 2027 return. Reference: Section 12 of the CGST Act and Notification 66/2017-Central Tax.

prompt: A beverage distributor in Karimnagar billed aerated drinks worth Rs 60,000 under the HSN code for packaged drinking water at 5%. What is wrong and what is owed?
completion:
The HSN code and rate are wrong. Aerated drinks fall under a different HSN and are taxed at 40%, not 5%.
Tax charged = 60,000 x 5% = Rs 3,000.
Correct tax = 60,000 x 40% = Rs 24,000.
Shortfall = Rs 21,000.
Issue a debit note with the correct HSN for the Rs 21,000, and pay it with interest at 18% a year from the original due date. Amend the HSN summary in GSTR-1. The buyer claims the extra Rs 21,000 as input tax credit (ITC), if eligible. Reference: Section 34(3) and Section 50(1) of the CGST Act.

prompt: An insurer billed an individual health policy with a premium of Rs 24,000 plus 18% GST in October 2026. Error?
completion:
Yes. Individual health insurance policies are exempt from GST from 22 September 2025, so no tax should have been charged on an October 2026 premium.
GST wrongly charged = 24,000 x 18% = Rs 4,320.
Issue a credit note for Rs 4,320 and refund it to the policyholder, or adjust it against the next premium.
Corrected premium = Rs 24,000 with no tax.
Group policies taken by employers remain taxable at 18%, so check the policy type before correcting. Reference: Section 34 of the CGST Act and the GST 2.0 exemption for individual insurance.

prompt: A soap manufacturer in Hassan is still charging 18% on toilet soap worth Rs 1,20,000 in November 2026. Fix the invoice.
completion:
Toilet soap moved to 5% on 22 September 2025, so the invoice over-charges tax.
Tax charged = 1,20,000 x 18% = Rs 21,600.
Correct tax = 1,20,000 x 5% = Rs 6,000.
Excess = Rs 15,600.
Issue a credit note for Rs 15,600 and refund or adjust it with the buyer. Corrected invoice total = Rs 1,26,000. Update the rate in the item master so future bills are right. The buyer reverses Rs 15,600 of input tax credit (ITC) when the credit note reaches it. Reference: Section 34(1) of the CGST Act.

prompt: A cement dealer in Tumakuru billed cement of Rs 2,70,000 at 28% on 10 October 2026. Correct it.
completion:
The rate is wrong. Cement has been at 18% since 22 September 2025, so 28% over-charges.
Tax charged = 2,70,000 x 28% = Rs 75,600.
Correct tax = 2,70,000 x 18% = Rs 48,600.
Excess = Rs 27,000.
Issue a credit note for Rs 27,000 against the 10 October invoice. Corrected total = Rs 3,18,600.
The credit note must be reported by 30 November 2027 for this financial year 2026-27 supply. Reference: Section 34(1) and Section 34(2) of the CGST Act.

prompt: We claimed ITC of Rs 2,34,000 on a car for our director and the credit was used from 20 July 2026. We reverse it on 18 November 2026. What do we pay?
completion:
Reverse Rs 2,34,000 and pay interest of Rs 13,963. Input tax credit (ITC) on motor cars for transporting people is blocked, so the credit was wrongly availed and used.
Days from 20 July to 18 November 2026 = 121.
Interest = 2,34,000 x 18% x 121 / 365 = Rs 13,963.07, rounded to Rs 13,963.
Pay the interest in cash. Add Rs 2,34,000 to the car's cost in the books. Reference: Section 17(5)(a) and Section 50(3) of the CGST Act.

prompt: A supplier invoice with GST of Rs 41,400 was booked twice and both claimed. The extra was used from 10 September; we reverse on 20 October 2026. Interest?
completion:
Interest is Rs 817 at 18% a year on the duplicate credit.
Days from 10 September to 20 October 2026 = 40.
Interest = 41,400 x 18% x 40 / 365 = Rs 816.66, rounded to Rs 817.
Reverse the duplicate Rs 41,400 in GSTR-3B and pay the interest in cash. Delete the duplicate entry in the purchase register, and reconcile it with GSTR-2B so it cannot recur. Reference: Section 50(3) of the CGST Act and Rule 88B of the CGST Rules.

prompt: We claimed Rs 58,500 ITC on an invoice that never appeared in GSTR-2B. Credit was used from 5 August; we reverse on 14 October 2026. What is due?
completion:
Reverse Rs 58,500 and pay interest of Rs 2,019. Credit is allowed only on invoices in GSTR-2B, so this claim was not eligible.
Days from 5 August to 14 October 2026 = 70.
Interest = 58,500 x 18% x 70 / 365 = Rs 2,019.45, rounded to Rs 2,019.
Once the supplier reports the invoice and it reaches GSTR-2B, re-claim the Rs 58,500 in that month's return, within the time limit. Reference: Section 16(2)(aa) and Section 50(3) of the CGST Act.

prompt: Our GSTR-1 for August 2026 missed an invoice with tax of Rs 72,000. We report it in October GSTR-1 and pay with October GSTR-3B on 20 November. Interest?
completion:
Interest is Rs 2,166 at 18% a year from the August due date.
August GSTR-3B was due on 20 September; tax paid on 20 November.
Days = 61.
Interest = 72,000 x 18% x 61 / 365 = Rs 2,165.92, rounded to Rs 2,166.
Show the invoice with its original August date in the October GSTR-1. The buyer gets input tax credit (ITC) only in the month it reaches GSTR-2B. Reference: Section 37(3) and Section 50(1) of the CGST Act.

prompt: Our accountant in Latur claimed ITC on GST paid for staff Diwali gifts, Rs 18,900, and the credit was used. Reversal on 24 November 2026; used since 20 October. What is due?
completion:
Reverse Rs 18,900 and pay interest of Rs 326 at 18%. Input tax credit (ITC) on goods given as gifts is blocked.
Days from 20 October to 24 November 2026 = 35.
Interest = 18,900 x 18% x 35 / 365 = Rs 326.22, rounded to Rs 326.
Pay the interest in cash. Book the gifts at cost including tax as staff welfare expense. Reference: Section 17(5)(h) and Section 50(3) of the CGST Act.

prompt: A seller in Nanded raised an invoice dated 1 November 2026 for goods actually dispatched on 26 October. Problem?
completion:
Yes. An invoice for goods must be issued before or at removal, so this invoice is late, and the time of supply is the dispatch date, 26 October 2026. That puts the tax in the October return, due on 20 November, not November.
Tax on Rs 1,80,000 at 18% = Rs 32,400, belonging to October.
If it is paid after 20 November, interest at 18% a year runs from 21 November until payment.
Report the invoice in the next open GSTR-1 and pay the Rs 32,400 with that interest. Reference: Section 31(1), Section 12(2) and Section 50(1) of the CGST Act.

prompt: Can an exporter avoid paying GST on exports?
completion: Yes. Exports are zero-rated, so an exporter can supply without paying integrated GST (IGST) by filing a letter of undertaking (LUT) each year. With the LUT filed, the export invoice carries no tax, and the exporter can claim a refund of unused input tax credit (ITC). Without an LUT, the exporter pays IGST and claims it back as a refund. For an export of Rs 9,60,000 at 18%, the LUT avoids blocking Rs 1,72,800 in tax until the refund arrives. Reference: Section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017.

prompt: How can we claim the maximum ITC legally?
completion: Claim every eligible credit on time and keep it safe. Reconcile purchases with GSTR-2B every month and chase suppliers who have not filed. Pay suppliers within 180 days so Rule 37 reversals do not arise. Claim blocked items only where an exception applies, and claim each year's credit by 30 November of the next year. For example, Rs 2,40,000 of eligible credit missed for March 2026 is lost if not claimed in a return filed by 30 November 2026. Reference: Section 16 of the CGST Act and Rule 37 of the CGST Rules.

prompt: Does the marginal relief rule mean I should avoid getting a small raise above Rs 12 lakh?
completion: No, you should not refuse a raise, but just above Rs 12 lakh most of it is lost to tax. New regime, FY 2025-26, taxable income Rs 12,10,000: slab tax = 20,000 (4-8 lakh at 5%) + 40,000 (8-12 lakh at 10%) + 1,500 (Rs 10,000 at 15%) = Rs 61,500. Marginal relief caps tax at the income above Rs 12 lakh, so tax = Rs 10,000, plus 4% cess Rs 400 = Rs 10,400. Without relief you would pay 61,500 x 1.04 = Rs 63,960. Because cess applies to the capped tax, a Rs 10,000 raise costs Rs 10,400 in tax, Rs 400 more than the raise. This only happens up to about Rs 12,70,588, where relief ends. Beyond that, every extra rupee is taxed at 15% plus cess. Reference: Section 87A (FY 2025-26); Section 156, Income-tax Act 2025 (from 1 April 2026).

prompt: How do we avoid 18% interest on ITC we claimed by mistake?
completion: Reverse it before it is used. Interest on wrongly availed input tax credit (ITC) arises only once it is utilised, meaning the credit ledger balance falls below the wrong amount. If you find Rs 64,000 of wrong credit and your ledger balance has stayed above Rs 64,000, reversing it now costs no interest. If it was used for 30 days, interest = 64,000 x 18% x 30 / 365 = Rs 946.85. Reconcile with GSTR-2B before filing GSTR-3B each month to catch errors early. Reference: Section 50(3) of the CGST Act and Rule 88B.

prompt: Can a company avoid GST on the salary of its whole-time director?
completion: Yes, lawfully. Salary paid to a whole-time director under an employment relationship is not a supply, so no GST arises, while fees paid to a director are under reverse charge. The test is how the pay is treated: as salary, with tax deducted at source (TDS) on salary under Section 392 (Section 192 for FY 2025-26) and a salary certificate, it is outside GST. Sitting fees, or commission booked as professional fees, carry 18% reverse charge. For a sitting fee of Rs 30,000, the company pays Rs 5,400. Reference: CBIC Circular 140/10/2020-GST.

prompt: Can we avoid tax deducted at source on a consultant if fees stay below Rs 50,000 in FY 2025-26?
completion: Yes. No TDS is needed on professional fees if the total paid to that consultant in the year stays at or below Rs 50,000. For example, fees of Rs 22,000 and Rs 26,000 total Rs 48,000, so no deduction applies. If a third bill of Rs 5,000 takes the total to Rs 53,000, deduct 10% on the whole Rs 53,000 = Rs 5,300 from that payment. Splitting one engagement into artificial bills to stay below the limit is not allowed. Reference: Section 194J of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

prompt: Can we avoid PF for a new manager joining at basic Rs 30,000 from December 2026?
completion: Yes, lawfully, if he is not already a PF member. A new joiner whose PF wages exceed the ceiling at joining is an excluded employee. From 17 September 2026 the ceiling is Rs 25,000 a month, and Rs 30,000 is above it. If he has an existing PF account from a previous job, he is a member and must be covered, with contributions of at least 25,000 x 12% = Rs 3,000 each side. Check his universal account number (UAN) history before deciding. Reference: paragraph 2(f) of the EPF Scheme, 1952.

prompt: We buy freight from a GTA. How do we avoid paying more GST than needed?
completion: The GTA decides the option, but you can ask for the one that suits your ITC position. A goods transport agency (GTA) either charges 5% with no ITC on its own inputs or 18% with full ITC, declared for the financial year; the 12% option ended on 22 September 2025. On a freight bill of Rs 1,20,000: 5% = Rs 6,000; 18% = Rs 21,600. If you can claim the tax as ITC, the extra Rs 21,600 - 6,000 = Rs 15,600 under 18% comes back as credit, so only cash flow differs. If you cannot claim ITC, for example because your own supplies are exempt, the 5% option costs Rs 15,600 less. Where the GTA charges 5%, you normally pay it under reverse charge as the recipient. Reference: Notification 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), GTA entry.

prompt: दिसंबर 2026 में एक कर्मचारी का basic + DA Rs 28,000 है। PF कितना कटेगा?
completion:
कर्मचारी का PF Rs 3,000 कटेगा और नियोक्ता भी Rs 3,000 देगा। 17 सितंबर 2026 से EPF की wage ceiling Rs 25,000 महीना है। नियोक्ता PF को ceiling तक सीमित रखे तो:
कर्मचारी का हिस्सा = 25,000 x 12% = Rs 3,000.
नियोक्ता का हिस्सा = 25,000 x 12% = Rs 3,000.
अगर कर्मचारी और नियोक्ता दोनों मिलकर पूरे वेतन पर PF चुनें, तो 28,000 x 12% = Rs 3,360 हर तरफ़ कटेगा। सितंबर 2026 से पहले के महीनों में ceiling Rs 15,000 थी।

prompt: मैं composition dealer हूँ। क्या मैं अपने बिल पर GST लिख सकता हूँ?
completion: नहीं, composition dealer अपने बिल पर GST नहीं लिख सकता और ग्राहक से टैक्स नहीं ले सकता। आपको tax invoice की जगह bill of supply बनाना है और उस पर लिखना है: 'composition taxable person, not eligible to collect tax on supplies'। उदाहरण: Rs 6,500 का माल बेचा तो बिल Rs 6,500 का ही बनेगा, कोई टैक्स नहीं। आप अपनी तिमाही बिक्री पर 1% composition tax अपनी जेब से CMP-08 में भरते हैं। अगर गलती से टैक्स ले लिया, तो वह सरकार को जमा करना होगा। Reference: Section 10 and Section 31(3)(c) of the CGST Act.

prompt: FY 2025-26, old regime: basic Rs 30,000 महीना, HRA Rs 12,000 महीना, किराया Rs 15,000 महीना, लखनऊ में। HRA में कितनी छूट मिलेगी?
completion:
HRA की पूरी Rs 1,44,000 की छूट मिलेगी। छूट तीन रकमों में से सबसे कम होती है:
1. मिला HRA = 12,000 x 12 = Rs 1,44,000.
2. किराया - वेतन का 10% = 1,80,000 - 36,000 = Rs 1,44,000.
3. लखनऊ metro नहीं है, इसलिए वेतन का 40% = 3,60,000 x 40% = Rs 1,44,000.
सबसे कम = Rs 1,44,000, इसलिए taxable HRA शून्य।
New regime में HRA की छूट नहीं मिलती। Reference: Section 10(13A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Rule 2A.

prompt: vetan 50,000 mahina hai, new regime, tax year 2026-27. TDS kitna katega?
completion:
Aapka TDS zero rahega. Saal ka vetan = 50,000 x 12 = Rs 6,00,000.
Taxable income = 6,00,000 - 75,000 standard deduction = Rs 5,25,000.
Slab tax: 4 se 5.25 lakh par 5% = Rs 6,250.
Rs 12 lakh tak ki income par rebate milta hai, isliye Rs 6,250 poora maaf.
Tax = Rs 0, toh Section 392 mein koi TDS nahi katega. Agar koi aur income milakar total Rs 12 lakh se upar jaaye, tab tax lagega. Employer saal ke end mein Form 130 dega.

prompt: salary 1,35,000 per month hai, new regime 2026-27. har mahine TDS kitna katega?
completion:
Har mahine lagbhag Rs 9,685 TDS katega.
Saal ki salary = 1,35,000 x 12 = Rs 16,20,000.
Taxable = 16,20,000 - 75,000 = Rs 15,45,000.
4-8 lakh 5% = Rs 20,000; 8-12 lakh 10% = Rs 40,000; 12-15.45 lakh 15% = Rs 51,750.
Slab tax = Rs 1,11,750; cess 4% = Rs 4,470; total Rs 1,16,220.
Mahina = 1,16,220 / 12 = Rs 9,685.
Yeh Section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 ke under katega aur Form 138 mein report hoga.

prompt: November 2026 mein basic + DA 18,000 hai, PF kitna katega?
completion:
Employee ka PF Rs 2,160 katega aur employer bhi Rs 2,160 dega. Basic + DA Rs 18,000 hai, jo 17 September 2026 se lagu Rs 25,000 ki ceiling se kam hai, isliye PF poori basic par lagega.
Employee 12% = 18,000 x 12% = Rs 2,160.
Employer 12% = Rs 2,160.
PF ka paisa agle mahine ki 15 tareekh tak, yaani 15 December 2026 tak, ECR file karke jama karna hai. Agar basic Rs 25,000 se upar hota, toh PF ceiling tak seemit rakha ja sakta tha.

prompt: Form 16 ki jagah ab kaunsa form milega? aur 12BB ka kya hua?
completion: Tax year 2026-27 se salary TDS certificate Form 130 hai, jo Form 16 ki jagah aaya hai. Income-tax Act, 2025, 1 April 2026 se lagu hai. Investment declaration ab Form 124 mein hota hai (pehle Form 12BB), aur pichhle employer ki salary details Form 122 mein (pehle Form 12B). Quarterly salary TDS statement Form 138 hai (pehle 24Q). FY 2025-26 aur usse pehle ke liye purane naam hi chalenge: Form 16, Form 12BB aur Form 24Q, Section 192 ke under.

prompt: transporter keh raha hai GTA 12% lagayega. abhi bhi 12% chalta hai kya?
completion: Nahi, goods transport agency (GTA) ke liye 12% ka option 22 September 2025 se khatam ho gaya hai. Ab do hi option hain: 5% bina input tax credit (ITC) ke, ya 18% poore ITC ke saath. Freight Rs 64,000 par: 5% = Rs 3,200, aur 18% = Rs 11,520. 5% wale option mein registered recipient aksar reverse charge mein tax bharta hai. Transporter se poochhiye ki usne kaunsa option declare kiya hai, aur usi hisaab se bill banwaiye.

prompt: debit note kab banana padta hai? galti se kam rate laga diya.
completion:
Jab invoice par value ya tax kam laga ho, tab debit note banta hai. Example: Rs 80,000 ke maal par 5% laga diya, jabki sahi rate 18% hai.
Laga tax = 80,000 x 5% = Rs 4,000.
Sahi tax = 80,000 x 18% = Rs 14,400.
Debit note = Rs 10,400 extra tax.
Debit note GSTR-1 mein report karein aur extra tax original due date se 18% interest ke saath bharein. Buyer Rs 10,400 ka ITC le sakta hai. Debit note ke liye koi time limit nahi hai. Reference: Section 34(3) of the CGST Act.

prompt:
User: A furniture maker in Sagar, Madhya Pradesh, sells a dining set for Rs 1,40,000 to a buyer in Sagar. What tax applies?
Assistant: Within the state it is CGST 9% + SGST 9%, Rs 12,600 each.
User: What if the buyer was in Gujarat?
completion:
For a buyer in Gujarat, charge integrated GST (IGST) of Rs 25,200 instead of central and state GST. The sale of the Rs 1,40,000 dining set from Madhya Pradesh to Gujarat is inter-state, so one tax, IGST, applies at the same 18%.
IGST = 1,40,000 x 18% = Rs 25,200.
Invoice total = Rs 1,65,200, the same as before.
The total tax does not change, only its type. Show Gujarat as the place of supply, and generate an e-way bill, since the value is above Rs 50,000. Reference: Section 7 of the IGST Act, 2017.

prompt:
User: What is the PF on basic + DA of Rs 22,000 for August 2026 if restricted to the ceiling?
Assistant: For August 2026 the ceiling was Rs 15,000, so Rs 1,800 each side.
User: Does the same apply from October 2026?
completion:
No. From wage months after 17 September 2026 the ceiling is Rs 25,000, so for October 2026 the full basic + DA of Rs 22,000 is below it. PF is then on Rs 22,000, not restricted.
Employee = 22,000 x 12% = Rs 2,640.
Employer = 22,000 x 12% = Rs 2,640.
That is Rs 840 more each side than the Rs 1,800 for August. Update payroll from the October run. Reference: Code on Social Security, 2020, and notification S.O. 5109(E).

prompt:
User: My salary is Rs 11,50,000, new regime. Is any tax payable for tax year 2026-27?
Assistant: Taxable income is Rs 10,75,000, fully covered by the rebate, so tax is nil.
User: My employer is adding a Rs 1,20,000 bonus in March. Now?
completion:
Tax stays nil even with the Rs 1,20,000 bonus, because taxable income remains within Rs 12 lakh.
Income = 11,50,000 + 1,20,000 = Rs 12,70,000.
Taxable = 12,70,000 - 75,000 = Rs 11,95,000.
Slab tax = 20,000 + 39,500 = Rs 59,500, fully covered by the rebate for income up to Rs 12 lakh.
Tax deducted at source (TDS) under Section 392 stays zero for March. A bonus above Rs 1,25,000 would take taxable income over Rs 12 lakh. The rebate would then go, and marginal relief would cap the tax at the amount of the excess. Reference: Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

prompt:
User: A pharmacy in Rewa bought stock with an invoice dated 4 May 2026 and has not paid yet. What happens to ITC?
Assistant: Unpaid after 180 days, ITC must be reversed under Rule 37.
User: The invoice was Rs 3,15,000 including Rs 15,000 GST. It paid Rs 2,10,000 on 20 October. How much to reverse?
completion:
Reverse Rs 5,000 of input tax credit (ITC), one-third of the tax. The 180 days from the 4 May 2026 invoice ended on 31 October 2026, and Rs 1,05,000 of the Rs 3,15,000 was still unpaid.
Unpaid share = 1,05,000 / 3,15,000 = 1/3.
Reversal = 1/3 x 15,000 = Rs 5,000.
Add it to output tax in the November 2026 GSTR-3B. Re-claim the Rs 5,000 when the balance is paid. Reference: Rule 37 of the CGST Rules.

prompt:
User: Our employee in Agartala gets HRA Rs 18,000 a month, FY 2025-26, old regime.
Assistant: The exemption is the least of three amounts.
User: Basic is Rs 40,000 and rent Rs 20,000 a month.
Assistant: Agartala is not a metro, so 40% applies.
User: So what is exempt?
completion:
The house rent allowance (HRA) exemption is Rs 1,92,000, so Rs 24,000 of the HRA is taxable.
1. Actual HRA = 18,000 x 12 = Rs 2,16,000.
2. Rent - 10% of salary = 2,40,000 - 48,000 = Rs 1,92,000.
3. 40% of salary, as Agartala is not a metro = 4,80,000 x 40% = Rs 1,92,000.
Least = Rs 1,92,000.
Taxable HRA = 2,16,000 - 1,92,000 = Rs 24,000.
In the new regime the whole Rs 2,16,000 is taxable. Reference: Section 10(13A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Rule 2A.

prompt:
User: A manufacturer in Kohima billed Rs 2,60,000 with IGST to a buyer in Nagaland.
Assistant: Within Nagaland it should have been CGST and SGST.
User: How do we fix it?
Assistant: Credit note for the IGST and a fresh invoice with CGST and SGST.
User: Do we pay interest on the CGST and SGST?
completion:
No interest is payable on the central GST (CGST) and state GST (SGST) when you correct tax paid under the wrong head this way. The law treats integrated GST (IGST) paid by mistake as a refund case, not as late payment of the correct tax.
CGST = 2,60,000 x 9% = Rs 23,400.
SGST = 2,60,000 x 9% = Rs 23,400.
Pay these, then claim a refund of the Rs 46,800 IGST within two years. Reference: Section 77 of the CGST Act, Section 19 of the IGST Act, 2017 and Rule 89(1A) of the CGST Rules.

prompt:
User: An employee in Bilaspur gets Rs 1,10,000 a month, new regime, tax year 2026-27.
Assistant: Annual tax with marginal relief is Rs 46,800.
User: He joined us only in October 2026 and had no earlier job this year.
Assistant: Then only six months' salary counts.
User: So what TDS do we deduct?
completion:
Deduct no tax deducted at source (TDS). With only six months' salary from October, his income is well within the rebate, so the Rs 46,800 full-year figure does not apply.
Salary October to March = 6 x 1,10,000 = Rs 6,60,000.
Taxable = 6,60,000 - 75,000 = Rs 5,85,000.
Slab tax = (5,85,000 - 4,00,000) x 5% = Rs 9,250, fully covered by the rebate.
TDS under Section 392 = Rs 0. If he declares income from an earlier employer this year in Form 122, recompute on the total. Reference: Section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

prompt:
User: Which form do employees use for investment declarations now?
Assistant: From tax year 2026-27, Form 124.
User: And for proofs relating to FY 2025-26?
completion: For financial year 2025-26, use Form 12BB, the old declaration form under the Income-tax Act, 1961. Form 124 replaced it only from tax year 2026-27, under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Both serve the same purpose: they list house rent allowance (HRA) claims with landlord PAN, leave travel, home-loan interest with lender details, and deductions such as 80C. For example, an FY 2025-26 claim of Rs 1,50,000 in 80C and Rs 2,00,000 home-loan interest is declared in Form 12BB.

prompt:
User: For a supply made in June 2026, until when can we issue a GST credit note?
Assistant: Declare it by 30 November 2027, or by the annual return date if earlier.
User: Does the same limit apply to a debit note?
completion: No. A debit note has no time limit for issue, unlike the credit note for the June 2026 supply, which must be declared by 30 November 2027. You can issue a debit note whenever under-charged value or tax is found, and pay the extra tax with interest from the original due date. For the buyer, the input tax credit (ITC) deadline follows the debit note's own date. A debit note dated December 2027 can be claimed until 30 November 2028. Reference: Section 34(3) and Section 16(4) of the CGST Act.

prompt:
User: We reversed Rs 9,600 ITC under Rule 37 because a supplier was unpaid after 180 days.
Assistant: You can re-claim it after paying.
User: We pay him in full in December 2026, two years after the invoice. Is it still allowed?
completion: Yes. You can re-claim the Rs 9,600 in the December 2026 return, even two years after the invoice. Rule 37(4) says the time limit of Section 16(4) does not apply to re-availing credit that was reversed earlier for non-payment. Show the Rs 9,600 as ITC re-claimed in GSTR-3B for the month of payment, and keep the payment proof linked to the original invoice. Reference: Rule 37 of the CGST Rules.
